O'Brien recalled: "To be genuinely sort of delighted that you'd been working for six months on this record and something great has come out of it, and you haven't contributed to it, is a really liberating feeling."^([26]) Jonny Greenwood described it as a turning point for the album: "We knew it had to be the first song, and everything just followed after it."^([28]) Yorke wrote an early version of "The National Anthem" when the band was still in school.^([28]) In 1997, Radiohead recorded drums and bass for the song, intending to develop it as a B-side for OK Computer, but decided to keep it for their next album.^([28]) For Kid A, Greenwood added ondes Martenot and sounds sampled from radio stations,^([28]) and Yorke's vocals were processed with a ring modulator.^([29]) In November 1999,^([29]) Radiohead recorded a brass section inspired by the "organised chaos" of The Complete Town Hall Concert by the jazz musician Charles Mingus, instructing the musicians to sound like a "traffic jam".^([30]) The strings on "How to Disappear Completely" were performed by the Orchestra of St John's and recorded in Dorchester Abbey, a 12th-century church about five miles from Radiohead's Oxfordshire studio.^([31][32]) Radiohead chose the orchestra as they had performed pieces by Penderecki and Messiaen.^([30]) Jonny Greenwood, the only Radiohead member trained in music theory, composed the string arrangement by multitracking his ondes Martenot.^([28]) According to Godrich, when the orchestra members saw Greenwood's score "they all just sort of burst into giggles, because they couldn't do what he'd written, because it was impossible – or impossible for them, anyway".^([33]) The orchestra leader, John Lubbock, encouraged them to experiment and work with Greenwood's ideas.^([34]) The concerts director, Alison Atkinson, said the session was more experimental than the orchestra's usual bookings.^([31]) "Idioteque" was built from a drum machine pattern Greenwood created with a modular synthesiser.^([28]) It incorporates a sample from the electronic composition "Mild und Leise" by Paul Lansky, taken from Electronic Music Winners, a 1976 album of experimental music.^([35]) Greenwood gave 50 minutes of improvisation to Yorke, who took a short section of it and used it to write the song.^([36]) Yorke said it was "an attempt to capture that exploding beat sound where you're at the club and the PA's so loud, you know it's doing damage".^([3]) "Motion Picture Soundtrack" was written before Radiohead's debut single, "Creep" (1992),^([37]) and Radiohead recorded a version on piano during the OK Computer sessions.^([38]) For Kid A, Yorke recorded it on a pedal organ, influenced by the songwriter Tom Waits. Radiohead added harp samples and double bass, attempting to emulate the soundtracks of 1950s Disney films.^([28][39]) Radiohead also worked on several songs they did not complete until future albums, including "Nude",^([40]) "Burn the Witch"^([41]) and "True Love Waits".^([42]) Music [edit] Style and influences [edit] [] "Kid A" The title track demonstrates the electronic processing prominent on Kid A. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ "The National Anthem" "The National Anthem" features a horn section improvising over a repetitive bassline. Yorke cited the jazz musician Charles Mingus as his main inspiration. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Problems playing these files? See media help. Critics identified elements of electronica,^([43][44][45]) post-rock,^([46][47]) art pop,^([48]) experimental rock,^([49]) ambient,^([50]) post-prog,^([51]) and electronic rock.^([52]) Though guitar is less prominent than on previous Radiohead albums, it was used on most tracks.^([3]) "Treefingers", an ambient instrumental, was created by digitally processing O'Brien's guitar loops.^([39]) Many of Yorke's vocals were manipulated with effects; for example, his vocals on the title track were spoken, then vocoded with the ondes Martenot to create the melody.^([3]) Kid A incorporates influences from electronic artists on Warp Records^([6]) such as the 1990s IDM artists Aphex Twin and Autechre;^([2]) 1970s Krautrock bands such as Can;^([6]) the jazz of Charles Mingus,^([30]) Alice Coltrane and Miles Davis;^([3]) and abstract hip hop from the Mo'Wax label, including Blackalicious and DJ Krush.^([53]) Yorke cited Remain in Light (1980) by Talking Heads as a "massive reference point".^([54]) Björk was another major influence,^([55][29]) particularly her 1997 album Homogenic,^([56]) as was the Beta Band.^([57]) Radiohead attended an Underworld concert which helped renew their enthusiasm in a difficult moment.^([58]) The string orchestration for "How to Disappear Completely" was influenced by the Polish composer Krzysztof Penderecki.^([2]) Jonny Greenwood's use of the ondes Martenot was inspired by Olivier Messiaen, who popularised the instrument and was one of Greenwood's teenage heroes.^([59]) Greenwood described his interest in mixing old and new music technology,^([59]) and during the recording sessions Yorke read Ian MacDonald's Revolution in the Head, which chronicles the Beatles' recordings with George Martin during the 1960s.^([3]) Radiohead also sought to combine electronic manipulations with jam sessions in the studio, saying their model was the German band Can.^([6]) Lyrics [edit] Yorke's lyrics on Kid A are less personal than on earlier albums, and instead incorporate abstract and surreal themes.^([60]) He cut up phrases and assembled them at random, combining cliches and banal observations; for example, "Morning Bell" features repeated contrasting lines such as "Where'd you park the car?" and "Cut the kids in half".^([61]) Yorke described the lyrics as "like shattered bits of mirror ... like pieces of something broken", and said he was not trying to communicate anything specific.^([7]) Yorke cited David Byrne's approach to lyrics on Remain in Light as an influence: "When they made that record, they had no real songs, just wrote it all as they went along. Byrne turned up with pages and pages, and just picked stuff up and threw bits in all the time. And that's exactly how I approached Kid A."^([3]) Radiohead used Yorke's lyrics "like pieces in a collage ... [creating] an artwork out of a lot of different little things".^([6]) The lyrics are not included in the liner notes, as Radiohead felt they could not be considered independently of the music,^([62]) and Yorke did not want listeners to focus on them.^([3]) Yorke wrote "Everything in Its Right Place" about the depression he experienced on the OK Computer tour, feeling he could not speak.^([63]) The refrain of "How to Disappear Completely" was inspired by R.E.M. singer Michael Stipe, who advised Yorke to relieve tour stress by repeating to himself: "I'm not here, this isn't happening".^([64]) The refrain of "Optimistic" ("try the best you can / the best you can is good enough") was an assurance by Yorke's partner, Rachel Owen, when Yorke was frustrated with the band's progress.^([6]) The title Kid A came from a filename on one of Yorke's sequencers.^([7]) Yorke said he liked its "non-meaning", saying: "If you call [an album] something specific, it drives the record in a certain way."^([5]) Artwork [edit] The Kid A artwork and packaging was created by Yorke with Stanley Donwood, who has worked with Radiohead since their 1994 EP My Iron Lung.^([65]) Whereas the pair had previously created album artwork through collage, photography and digital manipulation, for Kid A the
